title: deriveFactId's hash material uses an unescaped "|" delimiter (`${studentId}|${key}|${canonicalJson(value)}|${sessionId ?? ""}`); studentId and key are both unrestricted z.string().min(1) (packages/schemas), so a "|" inside either field lets two DIFFERENT (studentId,key) pairs derive the identical fact _id
evidence: direct read-only execution of the worktree's own packages/db/src/facts.ts via tsx (no edit made): deriveFactId("alice|X","c","v","s") === deriveFactId("alice","X|c","v","s") -> true (identical sha256). Consequence traced through applyApprovedDiff: activeFilter still matches on the real studentId/key fields (no false idempotent match), but the colliding _id would hit Mongo's built-in unique _id index on insertOne (E11000), and the subsequent re-read against activeFilter for the true (studentId,key) finds no matching doc, so the code falls to the else branch and throws FactConflictError for a legitimate, non-conflicting write -- a correctness gap, not a crash, and it requires a literal "|" character inside studentId or key, which nothing currently prevents.
fix: use a collision-safe encoding for the hash material -- e.g. hash each field separately and concatenate the hashes, JSON.stringify the tuple, or escape/length-prefix each segment before joining -- plus a regression test with a "|" embedded in studentId or key

title: resumeScribe forking from an already-resolved pre-approval checkpoint silently discards a second, DIFFERENT resume decision and replays the cached (original) decision instead, reporting success with the stale value
evidence: qa/verdicts/t-007-scribe-graph.md cycle 0 -- checker's own probe (scratchpad t007-probes/p3-fork-diagnostic.ts, run with tsx against the unmodified worktree, MockProvider + MemorySaver + fakes.ts, offline): after startScribe + resumeScribe({action:'approve'}) writes fact F (Canada), the checker fetched the pre-approval checkpoint id via getStateHistory and called graph.invoke(new Command({resume:{action:'reject', reason:'checker fork probe'}}), {configurable:{thread_id, checkpoint_id: pausedCheckpointId}}) directly. The raw invoke() return value shows decision:{approve:true, edits:[...the ORIGINAL Canada fact...]} and result.status:'written' with the SAME writtenFactIds as the first approval -- the 'reject' action was silently ignored. getStateHistory shows two sibling checkpoints forked from the same parent (the paused interrupt), both independently reaching the identical decision/result, proving the second branch's own counsellor_approval node execution did not honour the new Command.resume value. No B3 violation (no unapproved value is written -- the written value was genuinely approved once), but the reported outcome does not match the submitted decision, which is misleading (B14 concern) and untested by the maker's own D-012 fork test (which only ever resubmits an IDENTICAL decision, so it cannot distinguish real DB-layer idempotent replay via contentHash from LangGraph checkpoint-level caching of an already-resolved interrupt task).
fix: before T-008 (counsellor UI) or any retry/admin tool is built on ScribeRunOptions.checkpointId, add a test for the divergent-decision-at-same-checkpoint case and either (a) guard against it explicitly (throw instead of silently discarding the new resume value), or (b) document plainly in checkpointId's docstring that a checkpoint's interrupt resolution is one-shot / cached, and a second different resume value at the same checkpoint is not honoured -- callers needing a genuine 'redo the approval' must not reuse the same checkpoint id.

title: the per-round read-back in executeErasure is a sequence of independent countDocuments calls, not an atomic check; a writer that inserts a document for the student into a collection AFTER that collection's own residue count has already run in this round (but before the round finishes) is invisible to this round's totalRemaining -- if every other collection was already clean, the request is recorded completed (verified:true, totalRemaining:0, studentId+carriedSelectors unset) while the new document (and any edge to it) is permanently left in the database, unreachable by any future retry
source: checker cycle 1, own hostile probe (packages/db/tests/zz-checker-scratch.test.ts H4, plus two standalone repros zz-debug-h4.test.ts and zz-debug-h4b.test.ts -- all run via npx tsx --test, not part of the maker's suite, and deleted before commit)
reproduction: seed a confirmed request for stu-A. Hook students.countDocuments (the LAST step in ERASURE_PLAN) to, after computing the real count, seed a brand-new fact (studentId stu-A) plus its sourced_from edge, then return the pre-injection count. executeErasure(db, requestId) returns {status:'completed', receipt:{verified:true, totalRemaining:0}}, but fakeDb.collection('facts').all() and .collection('edges').all() still contain the newly-seeded fact and edge afterward. Reproduced a second way (zz-debug-h4b.test.ts): hooking scribe_resolutions.countDocuments (runs right after sessions' own count) to inject a new session + scribe checkpoint + session-kind edge produces the identical outcome -- verified:true, totalRemaining:0, status:completed, and the late session/checkpoint/edge all survive.
root_cause: src/erasure.ts:462-489: the read-back loop computes totalRemaining as the SUM of 9 sequential, independently-awaited countDocuments calls (one per ERASURE_PLAN step), evaluated only AFTER the whole loop finishes. A write landing in the gap between two of those calls -- specifically after its own collection's count already ran -- is not reflected in any line's `remaining` value for this round, so a fully-clean-looking totalRemaining==0 can coexist with real, unerased documents. Because this is the terminal state (verified:true breaks the round loop and commits completed, unsetting studentId/carriedSelectors), there is no later round or retry that could ever catch it.
fix: treat the read-back as no more trustworthy than the delete phases: before committing completed on a totalRemaining==0 round, re-resolve selectors fresh and run one more full confirmation read-back pass; only commit completed if that pass is ALSO clean, otherwise feed it back into the round loop (still bounded by ERASURE_MAX_ROUNDS) so carriedSelectors gets set correctly on eventual failure. A single one-pass 'sum of counts computed at different times' is not sufficient evidence of a clean state.

title: with the shipped default ERASURE_FENCE_GRACE_MS = 0, a fence-aware writer whose post-write check (compensateIfFenced) runs AFTER the fence's own release at completion is not caught: its write survives, the erasure's receipt falsely reports verified:true / totalRemaining:0 / status:completed, and studentId + carriedSelectors are unset on that same commit, so there is no automated retry path -- the orphaned personal data is permanent unless a brand-new erasure request is manually filed for the same student
source: checker cycle 2, own hostile probe (THE KEY PROBE, checker brief item 3)
reproduction: seedTwo() (real applyApprovedDiff-seeded student). Pause a real applyApprovedDiff writer at its own facts.insertOne (after its pre-check passes, since the pre-check would otherwise refuse it once the fence exists -- this is the only way a writer's insert can land at all). requestErasure + confirmErasure (sets the fence). Hook erasure_fences.deleteMany (the call releaseErasureFence makes for grace<=0) to, AFTER the real delete removes the fence document, release the paused writer and await its completion. Call executeErasure(db, requestId). Result: out.status === 'completed', out.receipt.verified === true, the writer's applyApprovedDiff call resolves { ok: true } (not StudentFencedError), and its fact + 2 edges are present in the fake collections afterward. A second executeErasure(db, requestId) call on the same request returns alreadyCompleted:true with the SAME stale receipt (totalRemaining:0) without re-scanning, and the row's studentId is already unset -- confirmed via a standalone repro script (zz-ckr2-permanence.mjs, run via npx tsx, deleted before commit) that the orphaned fact is still physically present after two executeErasure calls with no automated way to find it again.
root_cause: D-015's fence-plus-compensation design guarantees closure only for a writer W whose post-check runs WHILE the fence is up (W sees it and self-compensates) or whose writes all landed before the fence existed (so the purge's own resolve, which runs strictly after the fence is set, finds and deletes them). Neither disjunct covers a writer whose ENTIRE write completed before the fence, or straddles it, but whose post-check (a separate async DB round trip, isStudentFenced -> erasure_fences.findOne) is scheduled to run only after completion + release. With the default grace of 0, that window opens the instant the completion CAS commits -- there is no synchronization forcing every in-flight writer's post-check to run before that instant. This is documented by the maker as a known residual (manifest 'Fix cycle 2' Residuals section, and gate erasure-fencing Q1), but is shipped as the DEFAULT (ERASURE_FENCE_GRACE_MS = 0), not merely a configurable option a caller must opt into.
judgment: checker's ruling on item 3's question: a non-zero technical grace period (at least as long as the slowest fence-aware writer can realistically take) is REQUIRED for the fence mechanism to deliver B15's guarantee ('a verification pass reads back every collection and proves zero documents remain for that student') -- independent of the re-enrolment policy question gate erasure-fencing Q1 asks. Q1 frames grace length as a re-enrolment/UX tradeoff ('how long before this student can be written again'); this probe shows grace also does load-bearing CORRECTNESS work (closing the release-boundary race), which is a technical requirement the Approver's policy answer does not get to set to zero without reopening this exact gap. Shipping grace=0 as the default, with the request permanently losing its retry key (studentId, carriedSelectors) on completion, means B15's stated guarantee is provably false for this window, with no automated way to ever detect or recover the orphan.
fix: for fix cycle 3 (last cycle): either (a) ship a safe non-zero default grace bounded by a documented maximum writer duration (the existing gate erasure-fencing Q1 recommendation of 24h already covers this, so answering Q1 non-zero and changing ERASURE_FENCE_GRACE_MS's default closes this without new mechanism), or (b) do not unset studentId/carriedSelectors and do not treat the row as un-retryable at the instant of the completion CAS -- keep the retry key until AFTER the grace-delayed release has also passed a final confirmation read-back, so a completed-but-still-orphaned request can still be found and swept even at grace=0.

title: startErasureFenceSweep's tick() (erasure.ts) wraps options.onError?.(err) in a synchronous try/catch (the ISS-t-015-c0-3 fix), which only catches a SYNCHRONOUS throw from onError. An ASYNC onError (e.g. `async (err) => { await logToService(err) }`) whose returned promise rejects on a later microtask tick is NOT caught -- the rejection is discarded, unawaited, and surfaces as a real process-level unhandledRejection (reproduced via a live process.on('unhandledRejection') listener in a scratch-copy probe; the Node test runner itself flagged the async activity). ErasureFenceSweepOptions.onError's type, `(err: unknown) => void`, does not prevent this: TypeScript's structural typing allows a Promise-returning function to satisfy a void-returning function type, so a caller passing an async onError compiles without warning. Same failure class (unhandledRejection under Node's default policy, >=15, crashes the process) the ISS-t-015-c0-3 fix was written to close; only the synchronous half is closed. The shipped default (defaultSweepErrorLogger) is synchronous and does not exhibit this.
fix: await (or .catch-wrap) the onError call itself inside tick()'s try, e.g. `try { await options.onError?.(err); } catch { }`, or document loudly on ErasureFenceSweepOptions.onError that it must be synchronous / must never return a rejecting promise
fixed_by: t-017 cycle 1 (commit e44444d): tick() now routes onError through Promise.resolve().then(() => options.onError?.(err)).catch(() => undefined), returned so the outer .catch/.finally wait for it -- closes both the sync-throw and single async-reject cases. See ISS-t-017-c1-1 for a new, higher-severity gap this same change introduces (a never-settling onError).

title: startErasureFenceSweep's tick() cycle-1 fix (erasure.ts, for ISS-t-017-rev-2/ISS-t-017-c0-1) makes the outer `.catch(...).finally(() => { inFlight = false })` WAIT for onError's own returned promise chain to settle -- correct for the sync-throw and async-reject cases, but if onError returns a promise that NEVER settles (neither resolves nor rejects -- e.g. an async logging call with no timeout, hung on a stuck connection, exactly the documented/encouraged usage 'a caller SHOULD pass one wired to its logging'), the whole chain never settles either, so `.finally()` NEVER RUNS. `inFlight` is never reset to false, and every subsequent tick silently no-ops (`if (inFlight) return;`) -- forever, for the remaining life of the process, not just the failing tick. Empirically confirmed (scratch probe): onError was called exactly once; across 4 further ticks it was never called again -- the sweep is dead. Directly contradicts the code's own docstring ('so one bad tick never kills the interval OR the process'). No crash, no unhandledRejection, no log line, and nothing in this codebase monitors sweep liveness -- a silent, permanent halt of the B15 erasure-fence release mechanism. The shipped default (apps/api/src/index.ts defaultSweepErrorLogger) is a synchronous console.error and is not exposed; reachable only once a caller wires an async onError without an internal timeout, which is the documented usage pattern.
fix: race the onError call against an internal timeout inside tick(), e.g. Promise.race([Promise.resolve().then(() => options.onError?.(err)), delay(SOME_BOUND_MS)]).catch(() => undefined), so a hung onError can never block .finally from resetting inFlight. Add a test with a never-settling onError asserting the sweep recovers on a later tick.
fixed_by: t-017 cycle 2 (commit bd22ade): tick()'s onError call is now fully fire-and-forget -- constructed via Promise.resolve().then(() => options.onError?.(err)).catch(() => undefined) but never returned to/adopted by the outer .catch, so the outer .catch's own returned promise settles immediately regardless of what onError does, and .finally (which resets inFlight) always runs as soon as the sweep's own work settles. Verified via the manifest's 3 committed tests (never-settling promise, never-resolving thenable, non-function onError -- all confirmed the sweep recovers on a later tick) plus 4 independent checker probes (cycle 2): slow-then-reject, reject-on-Nth-call-only, sync-throw of a non-Error value, and a never-settling onError sustained across 300+ real ticks with a quantitative heap-growth check (--expose-gc: heapUsed delta was -0.03MB over 300 additional ticks, i.e. flat/negative -- the detached, unobserved promise chains are GC-eligible, not a retained-memory leak). Falsified: reverting erasure.ts to the cycle-1 (adopted-promise) shape reproduces the hang (the never-settling probe never completes; the sweep is provably dead), confirming the fix is load-bearing.

title: writeApproved's cycle-1 fix (nodes.ts, for ISS-t-017-rev-1) only compensates the summary on `err instanceof StudentFencedError` from applyApprovedDiff; a `FencedWriterDeadlineError` falls through untouched. applyApprovedDiff can only throw FencedWriterDeadlineError when its OWN compensateIfFenced post-check found the student NOT fenced at that instant (a genuine fence there throws StudentFencedError instead, which IS handled) -- so this is reachable only when an erasure is confirmed in the narrow window strictly AFTER that post-check ran clean. Reproduced in a scratch probe by seeding a real fence document immediately after intercepting that exact post-check's read: the summary survived on the row; in this probe's specific timing the run surfaced a raw FencedWriterDeadlineError rather than a clean {kind:'fenced'} (invokeFenceAware's own later, broader check raced the same narrow window too), but the load-bearing fact -- nothing compensates the summary on this path -- held either way. Non-blocking: self-heals via a caller retry (resumeScribe(null), idempotent per D-012) or, absent a retry, via executeErasure's eventual purge; same class as the T-016 manifest's already-accepted Residual 1/Residual 3 (narrow-timing, bounded, self-healing, no data corruption or unbounded residue); the manifest's own 'Open questions for the checker' flagged this exact scenario before shipping.

Verified via the manifest's 2 committed tests (fenced deadline-error -> undone; unfenced deadline-error -> kept) plus 2 independent checker probes (cycle 2): (1) the erasure_fences collection made unreachable (throws) on writeApproved's own re-check read -- confirmed fail-safe UNDO, matching compensateIfFenced/fencedForPostCheck's own 'unreadable = fenced' rule; (2) the undo's match-key (summaryApprovedAt) confirmed to touch only this call's own session -- an unrelated student's concurrent, unfenced, legitimate write on a different session is completely untouched. title: writeApproved's new FencedWriterDeadlineError branch (nodes.ts, ISS-t-017-c1-2's fix) re-checks the fence exactly once (isStudentFenced) before deciding whether to undo the summary. A fence confirmed strictly AFTER that single read (but before the function returns) is invisible to this re-check too -- structurally the SAME 'there is always a race after the last read' property every fence-aware check in this codebase already has (fencedForPostCheck, compensateIfFenced, recordApprovedSessionSummary's own post-check), not a new kind of gap, and bounded the same way D-016 already argues for every other writer: a write that lands before the fence is caught by executeErasure's purge (which only resolves selectors strictly after the fence exists), and B15's full hard-delete of the row is the absolute backstop regardless. title: B2/D-020 auto-verify surface has no negation handling: a country value cited to a quote that explicitly NEGATES it auto-verifies (needsReview: false) instead of staying flagged for the counsellor -- a wrong fact reaches 'verified'.
evidence: checker's own hostile-input run (throwaway copy, tsx --test), 2026-09-26: verifyCandidateFact({key:'targetCountry', value:'UK', source:{type:'transcript', quote:'UK nahi, Canada jaana hai', turnId:'t1'}}, ...) against a turn whose text IS 'UK nahi, Canada jaana hai.' returns needsReview:false (auto-verified) even though the quote literally negates UK. Same result for value:'USA' cited to 'Not united states, I want Canada.' -> needsReview:false. assessFactForReview/containsWholeWord/hasThirdPartyMarker (packages/engine/src/scribe/nodes.ts:249-320) never inspect any negation cue (no/not/nahi/never/kabhi-nahi etc.) -- the whole-word alias match fires regardless of what surrounds it besides the fixed THIRD_PARTY_MARKERS noun list.
fix: extend the review gate with a small, bounded negation-cue check (English no/not/never, Hindi/Hinglish nahi/mat/kabhi nahi) adjacent to the matched alias/number, analogous to hasThirdPartyMarker; any hit forces needsReview regardless of an otherwise-clean whole-word match. Add hostile tests for both directions (value affirmed vs. value negated) before re-check.
checker_note: checker cycle 1: independently reproduced fixed in a throwaway copy (git worktree add + pnpm install --offline). My own hostile-input probe (negation far from the value in the same turn, a double negative, Hindi/Devanagari negation post-position) all correctly return needsReview:true with reason negation:. Capability-coverage falsification (nodes.ts `const negated = ...` -> `false`) isolates exactly the named test ISS-t-013r-c0-1 plus one multi-reason test, reverted byte-identical (git diff clean).

title: D-020's third-party guarantee is bypassed two ways: (a) a bare pronoun referent with no relational-noun marker in the fixed lexicon, and (b) a Hindi/Hinglish kinship word not in the English-only THIRD_PARTY_MARKERS list.
evidence: checker's own hostile-input run (throwaway copy): quote 'He is in the UK, not me.' with value 'UK' -> needsReview:false (no marker word from THIRD_PARTY_MARKERS is present -- 'he' is a pronoun, deliberately excluded by design per the maker's own code comment). Quote 'Meri behen UK mein hai abhi.' (Hinglish: 'my sister is in the UK right now') with value 'UK' -> needsReview:false ('behen' is Hindi for sister and is not in THIRD_PARTY_MARKERS, which only lists English nouns). Both are genuine third-party-grounded values that auto-verify as the student's own, in a product whose own golden set (qa/evals/scribe/sessions.jsonl) includes Hinglish and Devanagari sessions.
fix: the pronoun exclusion is a reasonable design call against bare pronouns alone, but the lexicon gap for common Hindi/Hinglish kinship terms (behen/bhai/mama/chacha/didi etc.) should be closed given this product's stated user base; separately reconsider whether some pronoun signal is worth a narrow, bounded rule given D-020's 'at minimum' framing.
checker_note: checker cycle 1: independently reproduced fixed. My own hostile probe: 'mere bhai ko Canada jana hai', 'unka budget 20 lakh', Devanagari 'उनका बजट 20 लाख है' and 'मेरे भाई को कनाडा जाना है' all correctly return needsReview:true (reason third-party:). THIRD_PARTY_MARKERS now carries Hinglish/Devanagari kinship + pronouns as claimed. Falsification (`const thirdParty = ...` -> `false`) isolates ISS-t-013r-c0-2 plus directly-dependent tests, reverted clean.

title: resumeScribe forking from an already-resolved pre-approval checkpoint silently discards a second, DIFFERENT resume decision and replays the cached (original) decision instead, reporting success with the stale value
evidence: qa/verdicts/t-007-scribe-graph.md cycle 0 -- checker's own probe (scratchpad t007-probes/p3-fork-diagnostic.ts, run with tsx against the unmodified worktree, MockProvider + MemorySaver + fakes.ts, offline): after startScribe + resumeScribe({action:'approve'}) writes fact F (Canada), the checker fetched the pre-approval checkpoint id via getStateHistory and called graph.invoke(new Command({resume:{action:'reject', reason:'checker fork probe'}}), {configurable:{thread_id, checkpoint_id: pausedCheckpointId}}) directly. The raw invoke() return value shows decision:{approve:true, edits:[...the ORIGINAL Canada fact...]} and result.status:'written' with the SAME writtenFactIds as the first approval -- the 'reject' action was silently ignored. getStateHistory shows two sibling checkpoints forked from the same parent (the paused interrupt), both independently reaching the identical decision/result, proving the second branch's own counsellor_approval node execution did not honour the new Command.resume value. No B3 violation (no unapproved value is written -- the written value was genuinely approved once), but the reported outcome does not match the submitted decision, which is misleading (B14 concern) and untested by the maker's own D-012 fork test (which only ever resubmits an IDENTICAL decision, so it cannot distinguish real DB-layer idempotent replay via contentHash from LangGraph checkpoint-level caching of an already-resolved interrupt task).
fix: before T-008 (counsellor UI) or any retry/admin tool is built on ScribeRunOptions.checkpointId, add a test for the divergent-decision-at-same-checkpoint case and either (a) guard against it explicitly (throw instead of silently discarding the new resume value), or (b) document plainly in checkpointId's docstring that a checkpoint's interrupt resolution is one-shot / cached, and a second different resume value at the same checkpoint is not honoured -- callers needing a genuine 'redo the approval' must not reuse the same checkpoint id.
note: (checker, t-007 cycle 1) graph.ts:resumeScribe now reads the thread's latest state before resuming; if a decision is already recorded it returns already_resolved {decision, result, attempted} without invoking the graph. Independently reproduced beyond the maker's approve-then-reject/reject-then-approve cases: own probe for approve-then-EDIT-with-a-different-value at the same pre-approval checkpoint fork -> already_resolved, attempted.action=edit, decision carries the original approve, and the edited value (Germany) was never written. Also stress-tested with genuine Promise.allSettled concurrency (two truly concurrent resumes of the same still-open interrupt): the underlying write stays safe (D-012 idempotent dedupe, exactly one fact doc, no double-write, no mixed state) but a narrower race remains in the sequential guard itself, logged separately as ISS-t-007-c1-2 (non-blocking). Also confirmed the documented bypass (graph.invoke with a raw Command) is not reachable through @vc/engine's own exported surface -- Command/interrupt are not re-exported, only compileScribeGraph.

title: resumeScribe already_resolved guard has a TOCTOU race under true concurrency: two callers resuming the same still-open interrupt at once can both pass the getState pre-check and both be told a result that does not reflect their own submitted decision, with no already_resolved signal to the loser
evidence: qa/verdicts/t-007-scribe-graph.md cycle 1 -- checker's own probe (scratchpad checker-c1.ts, Promise.allSettled of two resumeScribe calls, one approve and one reject, on the SAME paused thread): both calls settled with kind=done, result.status=written -- neither reported already_resolved. The underlying data stayed safe (h.facts.size()===1, D-012 idempotent contentHash dedupe means only one fact doc could ever land, confirmed by reading back openFacts()), so this is NOT a B3 violation (no unapproved value was written) and NOT the sequential case ISS-t-007-c0-1 already fixes (getState-then-decide, called from two overlapping in-flight calls before either has recorded a decision, is a genuine TOCTOU window). But the caller who submitted reject was told status:written with no indication its decision was discarded -- the same class of reported-outcome-does-not-match-submitted-decision concern B14 warns about, one layer under the sequential fix.
fix: before any caller can issue concurrent resumes on the same thread (no current caller does -- T-008 does not exist yet), either serialize resumeScribe per-thread (an in-process or Mongo-backed mutex keyed on threadId) so the getState-then-decide check is atomic with the invoke, or accept the race and document it explicitly on ScribeRunOptions/resumeScribe's docstring so a future caller knows a losing concurrent resume is not distinguishable from a winning one by its own response alone.
note: (checker, t-007 cycle 2) graph.ts:resumeScribe now takes an atomic cross-process claim (insertOne into scribe_resolutions, _id=threadId, unique index on threadId, ISS-t-007-rev-8) before invoking the graph, closing the sequential getState-then-decide TOCTOU window this issue described. Independently re-verified with my own probes (scratchpad t007c2-checker-probes.ts), distinct from the maker's and the cycle-1 checker's own tests: 20 fresh-harness iterations of two concurrent DIFFERENT edits, 20+20 iterations of approve-vs-reject in both submission orders, and 20 iterations of 10 concurrent mixed resumes (edits/approves/rejects) plus an 11th late resume -- in every one of 300+ resumes across 60 races, exactly one caller is told done, every loser is already_resolved carrying the WINNER's decision (never its own), and the persisted state always equals the winner, with zero double writes. Stable across 5 repeated full runs. The prior finding (both callers told done/written) no longer reproduces.

title: (severity raised) concurrent resumeScribe on one thread: both callers get written, only one decision persists; a reject or a different edit is silently dropped and misreported as success
source: senior review T-007 cycle 1 (reproduced with Promise.all)
fix: atomic cross-process claim: a scribe_resolutions collection with a unique index on threadId; insertOne the claim before graph.invoke; the loser (11000) returns already_resolved with the winner decision; concurrent-resume test
note: (checker, t-007 cycle 2) graph.ts:resumeScribe closes the TOCTOU (senior Block, reproduced in cycle 1) with an atomic claim: an insertOne into scribe_resolutions (_id=threadId, unique index on threadId, no partial filter -- packages/db/scripts/db-init.ts INDEX_PLAN, confirmed by reading the plan directly) runs before graph.invoke; on 11000 the loser re-reads the winning claim and returns already_resolved with the WINNER's decision (never its own) and a sameAsWinner flag; the loser never invokes the graph, so there is one claim, one invoke, no double write. Crash-after-claim recovery: resumeScribe(null) resumes with the CLAIMED response when a claim exists and the interrupt is still pending, is idempotent on a second call, and a rival response in between gets already_resolved with result:null (winner still in flight) and the CLAIMED decision. Independently re-verified with my own probes (scratchpad t007c2-checker-probes.ts): edit-vs-edit x20, approve-vs-reject both orders x20 each, 10-concurrent-mixed x20 (300+ resumes, 60 races, stable across 5 full runs) -- exactly one done per race, every loser's decision matches the persisted winner. Own crash-after-claim probe confirms: a rival response gets already_resolved/result:null/the CLAIMED value; resumeScribe(null) completes the claimed decision; a second resumeScribe(null) is idempotent (no duplicate write). Own falsification (scratchpad t007c2-checker-falsify.py, F1/F2/F3) confirms each mechanism is load-bearing: disabling the insertOne, substituting the loser's own decision for the re-read winner's, and disabling the crash-recovery claim lookup each turn the relevant tests RED (fail=4, fail=5, fail=1 respectively); restoring returns engine 32/32 (scribe.test.ts) and the full suite 278/278 to green. title: executeErasure's final CAS update (both the verified/completed branch and the failed branch) discards the findOneAndUpdate result instead of checking it, so two concurrent executeErasure calls on the same confirmed request can both return success with a receipt that does not match what is actually persisted to erasure_requests
source: checker cycle 0, own hostile probe (packages/db/tests/zz-checker-scratch.test.ts H1, run via npx tsx --test, not part of the maker's suite)
reproduction: seed a confirmed request; Promise.allSettled([executeErasure(db, requestId), executeErasure(db, requestId)]). Both resolve with {status:'completed', alreadyCompleted:false} and different receipt objects (verifiedAt/startedAt differ), but only ONE write lands in erasure_requests (persisted row shows attempts:1, one specific receipt). The actual data deletion is correct and idempotent (B untouched throughout, read-back zero for A) -- only the RETURNED receipt vs PERSISTED receipt consistency is broken.
root_cause: src/erasure.ts:416-424 (verified branch) and :426-429 (failed branch) call erasureRequests(db).findOneAndUpdate({_id: requestId, status: row.status}, ...) and never check whether it matched. confirmErasure in the same file (:222-229) has the identical CAS shape but DOES check `if (!updated)` and re-reads/throws ErasureStateError on a miss -- executeErasure lacks that guard.
fix: in executeErasure, check the findOneAndUpdate result in both branches; on a miss (another concurrent call already transitioned the row), re-read the now-persisted row and return ITS stored receipt (with alreadyCompleted reflecting reality) instead of the locally-computed one -- mirror confirmErasure's existing pattern.
note: (checker, t-011 cycle 1) executeErasure's final CAS (src/erasure.ts:501-533) now checks the findOneAndUpdate result in both branches, mirroring confirmErasure's existing pattern. On a miss it re-reads the row: completed by a concurrent winner -> returns THAT run's stored receipt with alreadyCompleted:true and records nothing; still confirmed/failed -> records itself as the next attempt with merged carriedSelectors. Independently re-verified with my own probes (scratchpad t011-hostile-c1.test.ts H6/H7/H8, distinct from the maker's cycle-1 tests): 2-way AND 5-way concurrent success (all returned receipts deep-equal the persisted row, attempts stays 1, exactly one alreadyCompleted:false) and 5-way concurrent failure (attempts recorded 1..5 in sequence, final row equals the attempt-5 receipt, studentId+carriedSelectors retained for retry). This closes the gap; the returned receipt now always matches what is actually persisted at the moment it committed.

title: orphan edges survive erasure under a concurrent writer: factIds resolved once before the purge; a fact inserted mid-erasure is deleted by the broad studentId filter but its fact->sourced_from edge matches no selector; the run still reports verified:true and completes; the edge is permanently unfindable
fix: delete facts by the resolved _id list (not studentId), delete their edges, then re-count facts by studentId and loop until stable; or mark verified:false on any residue; red-then-green race test (insert mid-execute via stub)
note: (checker, t-011 cycle 1) src/erasure.ts's executeErasure now runs a round-based purge (ERASURE_MAX_ROUNDS=5): each round resolves selectors fresh and merges them (union, never shrinks) with every id seen so far; anchors (facts/sessions/scribe_resolutions) are deleted by the ids RESOLVED THIS ROUND (never a broad studentId filter), so a late-arriving anchor survives the round together with its dependents and is picked up by the next round's resolve; a failed/unstable attempt stores the accumulated ids as carriedSelectors, merged into the next retry since a deleted anchor cannot be re-resolved from the database. Independently re-verified with my own probes (scratchpad t011-hostile-c1.test.ts H1/H2/H3/H5, distinct injection points and scenarios from the maker's 3 rev-3 tests): a writer racing BEFORE phase 1 (at the first resolveSelectors read), BETWEEN phase 1 and phase 2 (new session+checkpoint+edge), MID phase 2 (an edge for a fact just deleted this round, plus a new session), and an unstoppable writer (bounded to between 2 and 10 rounds as required, ends failed+retryable, then a clean retry after the writer stops reaches verified:true with zero orphan edges) -- all 4 passed, orphanFactEdges()==[] and a full identifier scan ==[] in every case, with the other student untouched throughout. The specific delete-phase race this issue described is closed. NOTE: my own further probing (H4, during the read-back specifically) found a DIFFERENT, NOT-yet-fixed race in the read-back/verification step itself -- filed separately as ISS-t-011-c1-1 (high), out of this issue's original scope (which was about the delete phases, not the read-back).

title: the per-round read-back in executeErasure is a sequence of independent countDocuments calls, not an atomic check; a writer that inserts a document for the student into a collection AFTER that collection's own residue count has already run in this round (but before the round finishes) is invisible to this round's totalRemaining -- if every other collection was already clean, the request is recorded completed (verified:true, totalRemaining:0, studentId+carriedSelectors unset) while the new document (and any edge to it) is permanently left in the database, unreachable by any future retry
source: checker cycle 1, own hostile probe (packages/db/tests/zz-checker-scratch.test.ts H4, plus two standalone repros zz-debug-h4.test.ts and zz-debug-h4b.test.ts -- all run via npx tsx --test, not part of the maker's suite, and deleted before commit)
reproduction: seed a confirmed request for stu-A. Hook students.countDocuments (the LAST step in ERASURE_PLAN) to, after computing the real count, seed a brand-new fact (studentId stu-A) plus its sourced_from edge, then return the pre-injection count. executeErasure(db, requestId) returns {status:'completed', receipt:{verified:true, totalRemaining:0}}, but fakeDb.collection('facts').all() and .collection('edges').all() still contain the newly-seeded fact and edge afterward. Reproduced a second way (zz-debug-h4b.test.ts): hooking scribe_resolutions.countDocuments (runs right after sessions' own count) to inject a new session + scribe checkpoint + session-kind edge produces the identical outcome -- verified:true, totalRemaining:0, status:completed, and the late session/checkpoint/edge all survive.
root_cause: src/erasure.ts:462-489: the read-back loop computes totalRemaining as the SUM of 9 sequential, independently-awaited countDocuments calls (one per ERASURE_PLAN step), evaluated only AFTER the whole loop finishes. A write landing in the gap between two of those calls -- specifically after its own collection's count already ran -- is not reflected in any line's `remaining` value for this round, so a fully-clean-looking totalRemaining==0 can coexist with real, unerased documents. Because this is the terminal state (verified:true breaks the round loop and commits completed, unsetting studentId/carriedSelectors), there is no later round or retry that could ever catch it.
fix: treat the read-back as no more trustworthy than the delete phases: before committing completed on a totalRemaining==0 round, re-resolve selectors fresh and run one more full confirmation read-back pass; only commit completed if that pass is ALSO clean, otherwise feed it back into the round loop (still bounded by ERASURE_MAX_ROUNDS) so carriedSelectors gets set correctly on eventual failure. A single one-pass 'sum of counts computed at different times' is not sufficient evidence of a clean state.
verification_note: checker cycle 2: fixed by D-015 (erasure fence + post-write compensation). Re-reproduced the ORIGINAL attack with my own probe (real applyApprovedDiff, hooked on scribe_resolutions.countDocuments, a different injection point from cycle 1's) and the engine-level equivalent (real resumeScribe, hooked on students.countDocuments) -- both are now refused with StudentFencedError and leave zero residue. Falsified: disabling the writer's post-write compensateIfFenced call in facts.ts (mutate -> restore) turns the same probe red, confirming the fix is load-bearing. This exact reproduction (a write landing inside the SAME round's read-back, while the fence is still up) is closed. A narrower, DIFFERENT timing window at the release boundary (grace 0) remains -- filed separately as ISS-t-011-c2-1.

title: with the shipped default ERASURE_FENCE_GRACE_MS = 0, a fence-aware writer whose post-write check (compensateIfFenced) runs AFTER the fence's own release at completion is not caught: its write survives, the erasure's receipt falsely reports verified:true / totalRemaining:0 / status:completed, and studentId + carriedSelectors are unset on that same commit, so there is no automated retry path -- the orphaned personal data is permanent unless a brand-new erasure request is manually filed for the same student
source: checker cycle 2, own hostile probe (THE KEY PROBE, checker brief item 3)
reproduction: seedTwo() (real applyApprovedDiff-seeded student). Pause a real applyApprovedDiff writer at its own facts.insertOne (after its pre-check passes, since the pre-check would otherwise refuse it once the fence exists -- this is the only way a writer's insert can land at all). requestErasure + confirmErasure (sets the fence). Hook erasure_fences.deleteMany (the call releaseErasureFence makes for grace<=0) to, AFTER the real delete removes the fence document, release the paused writer and await its completion. Call executeErasure(db, requestId). Result: out.status === 'completed', out.receipt.verified === true, the writer's applyApprovedDiff call resolves { ok: true } (not StudentFencedError), and its fact + 2 edges are present in the fake collections afterward. A second executeErasure(db, requestId) call on the same request returns alreadyCompleted:true with the SAME stale receipt (totalRemaining:0) without re-scanning, and the row's studentId is already unset -- confirmed via a standalone repro script (zz-ckr2-permanence.mjs, run via npx tsx, deleted before commit) that the orphaned fact is still physically present after two executeErasure calls with no automated way to find it again.
root_cause: D-015's fence-plus-compensation design guarantees closure only for a writer W whose post-check runs WHILE the fence is up (W sees it and self-compensates) or whose writes all landed before the fence existed (so the purge's own resolve, which runs strictly after the fence is set, finds and deletes them). Neither disjunct covers a writer whose ENTIRE write completed before the fence, or straddles it, but whose post-check (a separate async DB round trip, isStudentFenced -> erasure_fences.findOne) is scheduled to run only after completion + release. With the default grace of 0, that window opens the instant the completion CAS commits -- there is no synchronization forcing every in-flight writer's post-check to run before that instant. This is documented by the maker as a known residual (manifest 'Fix cycle 2' Residuals section, and gate erasure-fencing Q1), but is shipped as the DEFAULT (ERASURE_FENCE_GRACE_MS = 0), not merely a configurable option a caller must opt into.
judgment: checker's ruling on item 3's question: a non-zero technical grace period (at least as long as the slowest fence-aware writer can realistically take) is REQUIRED for the fence mechanism to deliver B15's guarantee ('a verification pass reads back every collection and proves zero documents remain for that student') -- independent of the re-enrolment policy question gate erasure-fencing Q1 asks. Q1 frames grace length as a re-enrolment/UX tradeoff ('how long before this student can be written again'); this probe shows grace also does load-bearing CORRECTNESS work (closing the release-boundary race), which is a technical requirement the Approver's policy answer does not get to set to zero without reopening this exact gap. Shipping grace=0 as the default, with the request permanently losing its retry key (studentId, carriedSelectors) on completion, means B15's stated guarantee is provably false for this window, with no automated way to ever detect or recover the orphan.
fix: for fix cycle 3 (last cycle): either (a) ship a safe non-zero default grace bounded by a documented maximum writer duration (the existing gate erasure-fencing Q1 recommendation of 24h already covers this, so answering Q1 non-zero and changing ERASURE_FENCE_GRACE_MS's default closes this without new mechanism), or (b) do not unset studentId/carriedSelectors and do not treat the row as un-retryable at the instant of the completion CAS -- keep the retry key until AFTER the grace-delayed release has also passed a final confirmation read-back, so a completed-but-still-orphaned request can still be found and swept even at grace=0.
note: (checker, t-011 cycle 3, FINAL) fixed by D-016: every fence-aware writer now runs under an enforced WriterDeadline (FENCED_WRITER_DEADLINE_MS, driver timeoutMS + application abort), and the fence is never removed before createdAt + MINIMUM_FENCE_HOLD_MS (deadline + FENCE_MARGIN_MS), so a writer's post-check always runs while the fence still exists. Re-reproduced my exact cycle-2 KEY PROBE with independently written plumbing (own generic wrap of erasure_fences.deleteMany/updateOne rather than two separate closures): a real applyApprovedDiff writer paused before its insert, released only AFTER the genuine fence-release call returns (status confirmed 'completed' at that instant) -> StudentFencedError, zero residue. Plus 3 required variants: released after an explicit no-op sweep still inside the hold (still fenced), a writer that overruns FENCED_WRITER_DEADLINE_MS (aborted, bounded timeoutMS on every op, late-landing write undone via .settled), and a real resumeScribe writer released from a different erasure phase-1 step (edges.deleteMany) than any of the maker's or my own prior injection points -> fenced, zero residue. Falsified in a separate scratch git worktree (never mutating the reviewed worktree): reverting fenceReleaseTime/isStudentFenced to D-015's grace-only behaviour (dropping MINIMUM_FENCE_HOLD_MS) turns exactly this KEY PROBE red again (plus the maker's own KEY PROBE and 'no stuck fence' test), confirming the hold is load-bearing and this is the actual fix, not a documentation change. title: startErasureFenceSweep's tick() (erasure.ts) wraps options.onError?.(err) in a synchronous try/catch (the ISS-t-015-c0-3 fix), which only catches a SYNCHRONOUS throw from onError. An ASYNC onError (e.g. `async (err) => { await logToService(err) }`) whose returned promise rejects on a later microtask tick is NOT caught -- the rejection is discarded, unawaited, and surfaces as a real process-level unhandledRejection (reproduced via a live process.on('unhandledRejection') listener in a scratch-copy probe; the Node test runner itself flagged the async activity). ErasureFenceSweepOptions.onError's type, `(err: unknown) => void`, does not prevent this: TypeScript's structural typing allows a Promise-returning function to satisfy a void-returning function type, so a caller passing an async onError compiles without warning. Same failure class (unhandledRejection under Node's default policy, >=15, crashes the process) the ISS-t-015-c0-3 fix was written to close; only the synchronous half is closed. The shipped default (defaultSweepErrorLogger) is synchronous and does not exhibit this.
evidence: worktree t-017 qa/verdicts/t-017-residuals.md INDEPENDENT CONCURRENT CHECK (a708ee7)
fix: await (or .catch-wrap) the onError call itself inside tick()'s try, e.g. `try { await options.onError?.(err); } catch { }`, or document loudly on ErasureFenceSweepOptions.onError that it must be synchronous / must never return a rejecting promise
fixed_by: t-017 cycle 1 (commit e44444d): tick() now routes onError through Promise.resolve().then(() => options.onError?.(err)).catch(() => undefined), returned so the outer .catch/.finally wait for it -- closes both the sync-throw and single async-reject cases. See ISS-t-017-c1-1 for a new, higher-severity gap this same change introduces (a never-settling onError).

title: startErasureFenceSweep's tick() cycle-1 fix (erasure.ts, for ISS-t-017-rev-2/ISS-t-017-c0-1) makes the outer `.catch(...).finally(() => { inFlight = false })` WAIT for onError's own returned promise chain to settle -- correct for the sync-throw and async-reject cases, but if onError returns a promise that NEVER settles (neither resolves nor rejects -- e.g. an async logging call with no timeout, hung on a stuck connection, exactly the documented/encouraged usage 'a caller SHOULD pass one wired to its logging'), the whole chain never settles either, so `.finally()` NEVER RUNS. `inFlight` is never reset to false, and every subsequent tick silently no-ops (`if (inFlight) return;`) -- forever, for the remaining life of the process, not just the failing tick. Empirically confirmed (scratch probe): onError was called exactly once; across 4 further ticks it was never called again -- the sweep is dead. Directly contradicts the code's own docstring ('so one bad tick never kills the interval OR the process'). No crash, no unhandledRejection, no log line, and nothing in this codebase monitors sweep liveness -- a silent, permanent halt of the B15 erasure-fence release mechanism. The shipped default (apps/api/src/index.ts defaultSweepErrorLogger) is a synchronous console.error and is not exposed; reachable only once a caller wires an async onError without an internal timeout, which is the documented usage pattern.
fix: race the onError call against an internal timeout inside tick(), e.g. Promise.race([Promise.resolve().then(() => options.onError?.(err)), delay(SOME_BOUND_MS)]).catch(() => undefined), so a hung onError can never block .finally from resetting inFlight. Add a test with a never-settling onError asserting the sweep recovers on a later tick.
fixed_by: t-017 cycle 2 (commit bd22ade): tick()'s onError call is now fully fire-and-forget -- constructed via Promise.resolve().then(() => options.onError?.(err)).catch(() => undefined) but never returned to/adopted by the outer .catch, so the outer .catch's own returned promise settles immediately regardless of what onError does, and .finally (which resets inFlight) always runs as soon as the sweep's own work settles. Verified via the manifest's 3 committed tests (never-settling promise, never-resolving thenable, non-function onError -- all confirmed the sweep recovers on a later tick) plus 4 independent checker probes (cycle 2): slow-then-reject, reject-on-Nth-call-only, sync-throw of a non-Error value, and a never-settling onError sustained across 300+ real ticks with a quantitative heap-growth check (--expose-gc: heapUsed delta was -0.03MB over 300 additional ticks, i.e. flat/negative -- the detached, unobserved promise chains are GC-eligible, not a retained-memory leak). Falsified: reverting erasure.ts to the cycle-1 (adopted-promise) shape reproduces the hang (the never-settling probe never completes; the sweep is provably dead), confirming the fix is load-bearing.

title: writeApproved's cycle-1 fix (nodes.ts, for ISS-t-017-rev-1) only compensates the summary on `err instanceof StudentFencedError` from applyApprovedDiff; a `FencedWriterDeadlineError` falls through untouched. applyApprovedDiff can only throw FencedWriterDeadlineError when its OWN compensateIfFenced post-check found the student NOT fenced at that instant (a genuine fence there throws StudentFencedError instead, which IS handled) -- so this is reachable only when an erasure is confirmed in the narrow window strictly AFTER that post-check ran clean. Reproduced in a scratch probe by seeding a real fence document immediately after intercepting that exact post-check's read: the summary survived on the row; in this probe's specific timing the run surfaced a raw FencedWriterDeadlineError rather than a clean {kind:'fenced'} (invokeFenceAware's own later, broader check raced the same narrow window too), but the load-bearing fact -- nothing compensates the summary on this path -- held either way. Non-blocking: self-heals via a caller retry (resumeScribe(null), idempotent per D-012) or, absent a retry, via executeErasure's eventual purge; same class as the T-016 manifest's already-accepted Residual 1/Residual 3 (narrow-timing, bounded, self-healing, no data corruption or unbounded residue); the manifest's own 'Open questions for the checker' flagged this exact scenario before shipping.

Verified via the manifest's 2 committed tests (fenced deadline-error -> undone; unfenced deadline-error -> kept) plus 2 independent checker probes (cycle 2): (1) the erasure_fences collection made unreachable (throws) on writeApproved's own re-check read -- confirmed fail-safe UNDO, matching compensateIfFenced/fencedForPostCheck's own 'unreadable = fenced' rule; (2) the undo's match-key (summaryApprovedAt) confirmed to touch only this call's own session -- an unrelated student's concurrent, unfenced, legitimate write on a different session is completely untouched. title: Manifest capability-coverage row 4's stated falsifying edit is incorrect; the newly-added mid-cycle deadline-during-backoff block is unexercised by any test
evidence: packages/providers/src/index.ts:753-759, the NEW code added by this unit (inside FailoverProvider.generate's catch block: `if (remainingForBackoff <= 0) { lastError = new FailoverDeadlineExceededError(...); break; }`, replacing a bare `if (remainingForBackoff <= 0) break;`). The manifest's capability-coverage row 4 claims this block is 'logically falsifiable by reverting :756-761 ... which would leave lastError as the stale LiteLlmTimeoutError and fail the test's assert.equal(err.lastErrorName, "FailoverDeadlineExceededError", ...)'. Reproduced in a throwaway worktree: reverting ONLY this block (restoring the bare `break;`, keeping the OTHER T-032 fix at :737 -- the pre-attempt deadline check's `lastError = lastError ?? ...` -> unconditional -- intact) leaves the full suite at 49/49 GREEN, including the named test 'T-032 (ISS-t-021-rev-3): the deadline expires BETWEEN attempts (during backoff)' unchanged. Root cause: in that test, node:test's fake-timer tick(150) fires DURING the backoff `sleep()` wait, not before it starts, so `remainingForBackoff` (computed synchronously right after the failed attempt, before any sleep) is still positive and this new branch is never entered; when the pending sleep's timer fires and the while loop re-enters, the PRE-EXISTING top-of-loop deadline check (index.ts:737, already fixed by this unit) is what actually sets `lastError` correctly. Separately confirmed that reverting :737 alone (leaving the new mid-cycle block untouched) DOES redden this same test (actual='LiteLlmTimeoutError'), proving :737 is the code this test actually exercises. The mid-cycle block at :753-759 is therefore new, unreviewed-by-any-test production code: it may be correct for a genuinely distinct race (an attempt that consumes nearly all remaining budget before failing, so remainingForBackoff<=0 immediately, without going through raceDeadline's own timeout path), but no test in the suite demonstrates that scenario, and the manifest's own 'Open gaps' item 1 already flagged it was not falsified this session -- but asserted a specific falsification path that turns out not to work, rather than filing it as honest UNVERIFIED debt with an issue id.

owner: T-034 fix cycle (before any real drain scheduler is built)
summary: The drain query never uses the index built for it, and nothing purges delivered/dead rows, so drain cost grows with the ALL-TIME event count per tenant, not the pending backlog. outbox.ts:172-175 list() is find({}).toArray() with no filter and no sort; delivery.ts:170-172 fetches every document ever enqueued (full payloads, including delivered and dead) then filters pending/failed in application memory. The WebhookOutbox interface (outbox.ts:36-41) has no status-scoped query at all, so the {tenantId:1,status:1} index at db-init.ts:167-168 -- built explicitly for the drain scan -- is never queried and is dead weight. Fix: add list(status?) / listPending pushing the filter into find({status:{$in:...}}), same signature on InMemoryWebhookOutbox, so app-side filtering disappears.

owner: Umesh / cross-cutting B15-vs-B21 design question
found_by: data-engineer review (Warning; escalates the builder's own ISS-t-034-erasure-webhook-race from low)
summary: ESCALATION + SCOPE BROADENING of ISS-t-034-erasure-webhook-race. The ERASURE_PLAN webhook_outbox step (erasure.ts:1426-1430) deletes rows for a studentId regardless of delivery status, and nothing synchronises purge with drain. Under VC_ERASURE_AUTO_DELETE the loss is not a rare interleaving but STRUCTURALLY GUARANTEED: confirmErasure enqueues erasure.requested, reconfirm returns approved, the same handler calls executeErasure synchronously (server.ts:427) and deletes the row enqueued moments earlier in the same HTTP round trip; no drain exists to win the race. Consequence is a DPDP gap, not a lost notification: Pathlynks is never told to erase its own copy of a student the operator just erased. The broader un-logged case is identical for still-pending fact.approved events for any student later erased through the normal approver path (up to a 7-day window). DE rates high (builder logged low); not critical because it is behind a default-false flag, violates no B12/write boundary, and is logged rather than hidden. Do NOT enable VC_ERASURE_AUTO_DELETE against a real Pathlynks integration until this is closed.

owner: T-034 fix cycle (must land before any interval/cron wraps drainWebhookOutbox)
summary: No delivery-time claim or lock: two concurrent drainWebhookOutbox calls over the same tenant can both pick up the same pending record and both POST it. drainWebhookOutbox has no inFlight guard analogous to startErasureFenceSweep's (erasure.ts:971-973). Outbox bookkeeping stays consistent (findOneAndUpdate by _id), but the receiver gets the event twice and correctness rests entirely on Pathlynks deduping X-VC-Event-Id -- a contract delivery.ts:71-73 documents but never enforces or tests. At-least-once is a fine default IF stated as a decision; here it is an unstated side effect of a missing guard.
where: packages/engine/src/webhooks/delivery.ts:163-177 (no inFlight guard); pattern to reuse at packages/db/src/erasure.ts:971-973

title: B18 leak: packages/engine/src/cards/relevance.ts:202 '|| citedTopics.size > 0' lets a clarify card re-ask an ALREADY-KNOWN topic whenever it cites ANY known-topic profile fact, even an entirely unrelated one. The existing test cards-verifier.test.ts:138 ('building on a known fact ... is kept') cites the SAME topic it builds on, so citedTopics.has(topic) keeps it green.

note: PID-NAMESPACE CORRECTION + added falsification (checker safety-net pass, 17:08 real clock). (1) EVIDENCE CORRECTION to this row's original text: the clause 'PID confirmed NOT RUNNING by Get-Process' is WITHDRAWN as evidence. vc-testlock.sh records bash's $$, which in Git-for-Windows is an MSYS pid, NOT a Windows pid. Measured this pass: msys $$=263633 maps to WINPID 10012 (ps column 4); live bash Windows pids on this box are 4-5 digits (1556, 6636, 7472, 8736, 10856) while recorded owner values are 202605, 258793, 263913 -- and Windows pids are always multiples of 4, which none of those are. So Get-Process -Id <recorded-pid> can NEVER match a live owner: it returns DEAD unconditionally. The row's SUBSTANTIVE claim is unaffected and still stands, because it was established by reading both script copies, not by that probe: neither copy contains any owner-liveness code path at all; both break on age alone. (2) CONSEQUENCE FOR T-040, which is why this correction matters more than the original row: a helper that adds the obvious probe (Get-Process -Id $(cat owner)) would read every LIVE owner as dead and break the lock instantly, permitting concurrent test runs on a shared lock -- strictly worse than the age-only behaviour it replaces, and silent. (3) T-040's checker brief must therefore demand TWO falsifications, not one: (a) DEAD OWNER -- write an owner file naming a pid that does not exist and assert a waiter proceeds in SECONDS, not after the staleness window; (b) LIVE OWNER -- hold the lock from a genuinely running process and assert a second waiter does NOT break it and DOES wait. (b) is the one that catches the namespace bug; (a) alone passes while the lock is effectively disabled. The probe must query the same namespace the pid was minted in: kill -0 <pid> or ps inside MSYS, or record ps's WINPID if anything PowerShell-side will query it. Lock observed healthy and turning over normally during this pass (holder maker-t010-c2 263793 -> 263913 within ~3 min, T-010 cycle-2 verify live), so this is a design finding, not an incident.

title: T-043's 'repo-file-arg' narrowing shape ('pnpm -r (test|typecheck) -- <path>') is functionally inert -- the <path> argument never restricts what runs, so 69 of 125 (55.2%) fixed/verified rows now marked conforming carry a regression_check indistinguishable in practice from the bare whole-suite command ISS-076's own prior sweep explicitly rejected as inadequate
evidence: Checker t-043 cycle-0 review, own runs in D:/vc/.worktrees/t-043-regression-check-conformance. (1) `pnpm -r test -- packages/engine/tests/index.test.ts` produces byte-identical package-level counts to a plain `pnpm -r test` with no argument at all: both runs show packages/engine test tests=689 pass=644 fail=0, and both full logs are 1422 lines (saved to /tmp/repofilearg_run.log and /tmp/plain_run.log). Repeated for packages/db with `-- packages/db/tests/erasure.test.ts`: again tests=248 pass=248 fail=0, identical to the plain run. (2) Root cause: every package's own "test" script is a shell glob (packages/engine: "tsx --test tests/*.test.ts evals/*.test.ts"; packages/db: "tsx --test tests/*.test.ts"). pnpm passes the trailing `-- <path>` arg to EVERY workspace's test script unchanged; the glob already expands to the package's full file set before the extra path is appended, so node's test runner just runs (glob-matched files) + (one more path), never fewer. The path is therefore decorative. (3) Confirmed the checker's own instrument (scripts/vc-regression-check-conformance.py, RE_REPO_FILE_ARG) validates ONLY that the path string exists on disk -- not that it is a test file, not that it narrows anything: a synthetic row `{"id":"PROBE-1","status":"fixed","regression_check":"pnpm -r test -- ARCHITECTURE.md"}` (a doc, not a test) is reported `conforming: 1/1 (100.0%)` by the maker's own script, and actually running that exact command still executes the full 689-test engine suite unchanged. (4) Impact count: `python3 -c` field-merge over the current qa/issues.jsonl shows 69/125 fixed/verified rows use this shape (regex ^pnpm -r (test|typecheck) -- ). None of these 69 rows' regression_check can be trusted to isolate a revert-introduced regression to the specific fix it claims to cover -- reproducing it is really 'rerun the whole monorepo suite,' the exact class T-043's own manifest calls out ISS-076's prior sweep as having correctly flagged ('BARE allowlist command, no test-file argument ... non-conforming') before this shape existed to disguise it with an inert path suffix. (5) B14 gap: scripts/vc-regression-check-conformance.test.sh Test 3 and Test 15 (the repo-file-arg cases) only assert the checker's conforms_one() return value against a fixture path -- neither test ever executes the resulting shell command, so this inertness was never caught by the unit's own 19-case/30-assertion suite.
note: Blocks t-043-regression-check-conformance cycle-0 PASS. Fix must make repo-file-arg either (a) genuinely narrow -- e.g. pass the path through node:test's own file-selection semantics correctly (verify empirically, the way this finding did, that a differing path changes which tests execute), or (b) be retired in favour of package-filter/package-dir (which DO narrow, verified: they invoke the target package's own test script only) plus a real --test-name-pattern-style shape for sub-file narrowing, which the unit's own Open Gaps section already flagged as unaddressed. Re-classifying the 69 affected rows (are they package-filter-equivalent, or do they in fact need the coarse whole-suite command they were dressed up to avoid) is also required before ISS-076 can be honestly called closed.

Checker t-043 cycle-0 verdict: FAIL, not closed. T-043 correctly diagnosed the root cause (no per-package/per-file narrowing convention existed) and 5 of its 6 new shapes (package-filter, package-dir, direct-tsx, doc-grep, and the null bucket) hold up under independent re-derivation and spot-checks. But the single most-used new shape, repo-file-arg (`pnpm -r (test|typecheck) -- <path>`), is functionally inert -- verified empirically (see ISS-092): the trailing path never narrows execution, so 69/125 (55.2%) of the rows T-043 marks 'conforming' still carry, in practice, the same un-narrowed whole-suite check the prior sweep already flagged as inadequate ('BARE allowlist command, no test-file argument'), just with a cosmetic path suffix the checker script validates for existence only. The reported before/after (109/125 -> 125/125) is real arithmetic against T-043's own instrument, but that instrument does not actually verify the property ISS-076 cares about (a regression_check that can fail when its fix is reverted AND is specific enough to attribute the failure to that fix) for the majority shape. fixed -> verified is therefore still not honestly unblocked for those 69 rows. Independent reproduction of the original '50/120 (41.6%)' figure: not cleanly reproducible with a single well-defined script -- a strict verbatim-3-commands reading gives 115/125 (92.0%) non-conforming, a charitable reading that also tolerates the (inert) repo-file-arg shape gives 46/125 (36.8%) -- both are the right order of magnitude but neither lands exactly on 50/120, confirming the original figure was itself a manual/judgment-based re-derivation, not a reproducible machine check; this is consistent with, not contradictory to, ISS-076's own root-cause diagnosis. See qa/verdicts/t-043-regression-check-conformance.md for the full analysis.

INSTANCE 2, qa/gates/t-010-b1-b18-unsatisfiable.md, fixed at 999fc49, found by vc-30's own sweep of all five gates and NOT by me: that gate carried TWO COMPETING ANSWER SURFACES -- an (a)/(b)/(c) options block written when the gate opened, and four decisions D1-D4 written after the stall diagnosis landed. Verified the repair: D1-D4 is now marked the authoritative answer surface, the note sits at lines 57-61 ABOVE the options so a top-down reader meets it first, and the options are relabelled 'context for D1-D2 -- not the answer surface'. WHY INSTANCE 2 IS THE WORSE ONE: ISS-098 offered a wrong ANSWER; this offered a wrong QUESTION. A wrong answer is catchable by anyone who reads the file's own measurements; a wrong question is not, because both surfaces look correct in isolation and neither contradicts the other on its face. It had also been live longer -- the maker was reporting 'blocked on D1+D2' to Umesh while the file's first answer surface asked him to pick a letter, so the two halves of the pair were describing different gates to the same human. SWEEP VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY, not taken on report: the other three gates each have exactly one options block and three letter options. b18-unimplemented's appended 'Claim CONFIRMED independently' section sharpens option (a) but states explicitly 'Unchanged: the question, the three options, and the recommendation', so it is sound; auto-verify-surface's only later section is a Relayed (UNCONFIRMED) note, which is a provenance record and not a competing surface; p2-application-drafting-scope has no later sections at all. THE CLASS IS NOW THREE DEEP AND HAS LEFT THE TOOLING ENTIRELY: ISS-056 in a hook's reader, ISS-098 instance 1 in a gate's options, instance 2 in a gate's question. One mechanism throughout -- a correction is appended, the superseded statement is left standing, and whoever reads top-down gets the pre-correction answer. In code a max-cycle reader fixes it (ISS-095). IN PROSE NO READER FIX REACHES IT, and the only defence that worked on either instance was a session re-reading the whole file rather than the diff -- instance 1 came from me reading a gate I had no unit in, instance 2 from vc-30 sweeping four gates it had not been asked about. title: The checker's own ledger-size figures were wrong all evening -- 479/480/483 reported against 578 actual records -- so every count this session published about its own canonical file was understated by ~95
evidence: Caught at 2026-09-28T00:15 IST while re-measuring ISS-084's inflation ratio instead of copying the gate's figure. Byte-level measurement is authoritative and unambiguous: 600514 bytes, 578 LF, 578 CRLF, 0 lone CR, file ends with a newline, 578 non-empty LF-separated records, 578/578 parse as JSON. Text-mode iteration in a fresh process agrees: 578. But the validation tail appended to every one of this session's write scripts printed `lines 479`, `480`, `481`, `482`, `483` across the evening, and those numbers were reported to the user and to the peer session each time. The row count was wrong; the `parse_failures 0` half of the same line was right and is now independently confirmed at 578/578. The appends themselves all landed -- `git show HEAD:qa/issues.jsonl` contains this session's row bodies (`SCOPE BOUND TO ISS-097`, `BOTH INSTANCES FIXED AND BOTH VERIFIED`), so nothing was lost and no write went to the wrong file; only the reported size was false. A SECOND instrument failure surfaced in the same minute and is the more embarrassing one: `grep -c '"id":"ISS-095"'` returned 0 for a row that is demonstrably present, because `json.dumps` writes `{"id": "ISS-095"` WITH A SPACE after the colon and the grep pattern had none. A zero from that grep reads exactly like `row absent`.
note: ID COLLISION AVOIDED ON WRITE: this row was drafted as ISS-099 and renumbered to ISS-101 before its commit, because vc-30's T-043 cycle-2 checker had independently minted ISS-099 (a third Goodhart species -- coverage-absence) and ISS-100 (cross-branch ledger copying) in the same two minutes, committed at 66bad91. Theirs came first and keeps the number. Worth recording as a finding in its own right: two writers picked the SAME next id within ~120 seconds because each derived it from the highest id it could see, and a checker subagent on a wave branch cannot see a row the standing checker has not committed yet. Nothing was lost here only because mine was still uncommitted when I noticed. The ledger is nominally single-writer, but a dispatched checker subagent writes its own findings by protocol, so 'single writer' is false in practice during any live check -- allocate ids by reading the file at write time and re-checking after a merge, never from a number remembered earlier in a session. I cannot reproduce how the 483 arose -- the loop as written (`for l in open(f): if l.strip(): n+=1`) yields 578 when re-run against the same committed bytes, git status is clean, and no commit after 991facc touched the file -- so I am NOT offering a mechanism. What I will state is the finding: the instrument was unreliable, the byte-level count supersedes it, and the numbers I published were wrong. Filed rather than quietly corrected because the count went into user-facing reports and into two cross-session messages, and because an unexplained instrument is worse than a diagnosed one, not better. THE SAME CLASS AGAIN, and this is the fifth and sixth instance in about seven hours: ISS-056 (a reader taking any Status line), ISS-095 (three readers of `Cycle checked` -- bare-anchor, first-wins, last-wins -- all wrong), ISS-097 (a reader looking for a verdict only beside its manifest), ISS-098 x2 (a gate offering a refuted option, and a gate with two competing answer surfaces), and now these two: a size counter nobody validated and a grep whose pattern did not match its own writer's spacing. EVERY instance is the same shape -- a reader written against an ASSUMED format, producing a plausible number, with no independent check that the number is right. The zero-grep is the purest form of it and repeats this morning's lesson exactly: an empty result is a claim about the instrument before it is a claim about the file (see the memory note `readers-must-match-writer-format`). PRACTICAL RULES this session should have been following and now will: (1) never report a count from the same loop that wrote the file -- measure from bytes, in a separate process; (2) grep the ledger by `"id":\s*"<id>"`, never with assumed spacing, or better, parse it as JSON; (3) treat any zero or any round-looking count as unverified until a second, differently-written instrument agrees. WHAT IS TRUE NOW, all byte-verified: 578 records, 277 distinct ids, 0 parse failures, 284 raw `status==open` lines against 138 genuinely open ids (2.06x inflation, which is the corrected figure for ISS-084's gate), 388 partial rows carrying only changed fields, 179 rows with no `severity`, and 122 ids whose severity is silently dropped by a last-row-wins reader. Open by severity, entity-resolved: 20 high, 50 medium, 67 low, 1 low-medium.

WITHDRAWN -- THE CENTRAL CLAIM WAS FALSE AND THE INSTRUMENT WAS RIGHT. I filed this an hour ago saying my per-write row counter had understated the ledger all evening (479/480/483 against 578) and that I could offer no mechanism. Both halves were wrong, and the mechanism was available the whole time from `git show <commit>:qa/issues.jsonl | grep -c .`, which I did not run before filing. Measured across every commit this session authored: 20b70c8=453, f7f5260=470, 3cf442a=474, 8777126=475, e2aa4fd=476, 14d2f3e=477, d4af250=478, 99df513=479, 15caba3=480, 7f71553=481, 0b862b8=482, 991facc=483. Every number I reported matches the committed file exactly at the moment I reported it. Nothing was understated. WHAT ACTUALLY GREW THE FILE was the T-043 merge: 486 rows on main at 66bad91, 578 immediately after `ee95e0c`, so the wave branch contributed ~92 rows. That is ISS-100's defect -- cycles 1 and 2 hand-copied already-committed main rows into the branch -- not a reader defect at all, and vc-30 had already diagnosed and filed it before I mistook its effect for my own bug. Then `e95c204` removed 5 byte-identical lines (573) and my own ISS-101 append made 574. RECONCILING THE PEER'S RECONCILIATION, since it is also not right: vc-30 explained my 574 as a pre-merge-main measurement. It was not -- I measured after the dedupe and reported `HEAD: 573, worktree: 574` in the same breath, the extra row being my own uncommitted one. The count the sweep must re-derive against is therefore 574, not 573, and 573 was already stale when it was written down. THE ONE REAL DEFECT IN THAT ROW SURVIVES and is why this is `wontfix` rather than deleted: `grep '"id":"ISS-095"'` returns 0 for a present row because `json.dumps` emits `"id": ` with a space. That is a genuine reader/writer format mismatch, it is the same class as ISS-095/096/097/098, and it stays on the record. WHY I GOT THIS WRONG, which is the part worth keeping: five instances of one bug class in seven hours had made the class itself the expected answer, so when two numbers disagreed I reached for 'my reader is broken' without running the one command that distinguishes a bad reader from a changed file. A pattern that has been right five times running is precisely when it stops being evidence. Filing a self-accusation is not automatically rigour -- an unexplained finding I published and then had to withdraw cost more than the ten seconds of `git show` would have.

SCOPE MEASURED, and it is ~17x larger than the 5 lines the merge gate caught. The `e95c204` dedupe removed 5 byte-identical repeats (ISS-092, ISS-093, ISS-094, two ISS-076 updates). But comparing pre-merge main (66bad91, 486 rows) against the post-merge ledger by exact row content: 88 rows exist now that did not exist on main, and only ONE new id was introduced (ISS-101, mine). So roughly 87 of those rows are additional copies of rows already recorded for existing ids -- branch-side duplicates whose fields differ just enough to escape a byte-identical check. The ledger is therefore ~15% noise by row count, which is what made the file jump 486 -> 578 and what I briefly and wrongly attributed to my own counter (see ISS-101, withdrawn). NO HARM DONE THIS TIME, verified rather than assumed: entity-resolving both revisions and comparing status per id, ZERO ids regressed (`open <- fixed/verified`). That is luck about field content, not a property of the process -- the merge-order resolution this ledger depends on means a stale copy landing after a newer row WOULD silently revert that id's state, and nothing in the current gate would catch it, because the gate tests for identical lines and these are not identical. STRENGTHEN THE GATE TO MATCH THE DEFECT: ISS-100's merge check should compare entity-resolved state before and after a merge and fail on any backwards status transition, rather than grepping for duplicate lines. That is a real invariant and it is cheap -- the comparison above took one script. Also worth stating so the next merge does not relearn it: the fix for the root cause is that a wave branch must never copy committed ledger rows from main; a checker subagent appends only its OWN new rows, and the merge brings exactly those.

SCOPE CORRECTION, and the gate instrument was wrong. This row was filed as 'the merge produces duplicate ISS-093/ISS-094 lines' and was closed at e95c204 by removing 5 byte-identical rows. That measured the wrong thing. Entity-resolving 66bad91 (pre-merge main, 486 rows) against HEAD (576): 90 rows are not present pre-merge and exactly ONE is a new id (ISS-101). ~89 are near-duplicate re-copies of rows already recorded, differing in whitespace or field subsets, invisible to a byte-identical check. Ledger is ~15% noise by row count. NO DAMAGE OCCURRED and that is luck, not a property: latest-row-per-id merge before vs after shows zero ids regressed closed->open and no pre-merge id is missing. But merge-order resolution means a stale copy landing after a newer row silently reverts that id's state, and the byte-identical gate cannot see it. REMEDY: the merge gate must compare entity-resolved status before and after a merge and fail on any backwards transition. ROOT CAUSE unchanged: a wave branch must never copy committed rows from main; a checker subagent appends only its own new rows. Found by peer session vc-f5 (157d859); both the row counts and the entity-resolved comparison independently reproduced here before recording.
severity_reason: raised from the merge-hazard framing: the hazard is silent state reversion, not duplicate text
found_by: vc-f5, independently reproduced by the maker

title: This Mode B sweep ran against a live moving target: a peer session committed to qa/issues.jsonl, qa/QUEUE.md and qa/gates/hook-raw-count-fixes.md at least 9 times during the sweep (ff7c512 through fcea4b7), with no lock or hand-off protocol for a shared append-only ledger during an active sweep
evidence: git rev-parse HEAD read three separate times during this sweep returned ff7c512, then 2063b9b, then fcea4b7 -- each time issues.jsonl's own row count and max id had moved (574 -> 576 -> 577; max plain ISS id 100 -> 101). SKILL.md 'If a project runs a standing checker session anyway' already names the exact risk class ('two live sessions sharing a directory deadlocked in the wild, 2026-08-17'); this sweep did not deadlock, but only because both writers happened to touch disjoint fields each time. No damage this time is luck, not a property -- there is no compare-and-swap or lock analogous to scripts/vc-testlock.sh (T-040) protecting qa/issues.jsonl itself.

title: The VERDICT declaration itself (not just Cycle checked, ISS-095's scope) has at least 4 incompatible writer shapes across qa/verdicts/*.md, and a naive automated reconciliation of manifest Status vs verdict outcome produces false PASS/FAIL mismatches
evidence: Observed shapes: (1) '**Verdict:** PASS' (t-006-mcp-servers.md:3); (2) 'VERDICT: PASS' / '## VERDICT: PASS' at line-start (t-043-regression-check-conformance.md:387, matches the SKILL.md return-block grammar); (3) '## Verdict: PASS' as a one-line heading (t-037-failover-cancellation.md, search: '## Verdict'); (4) a bare '## Verdict' heading with the value 'PASS.' as the next paragraph (t-029-erasure-approver.md:90-92). Separately, qa/verdicts/t-017-residuals.md reverses the usual Cycle-then-Verdict field order (Verdict declared BEFORE Cycle checked, lines 3-4) and is written newest-first, the same file ISS-095/hook-raw-count-fixes.md already names for the Cycle-checked defect. I wrote a first-pass block-boundary parser during this sweep that mis-paired cycle numbers with verdicts on 5 units (t-004, t-013, t-017, t-032, t-042 all showed as false 'checked-PASS but max-cycle verdict FAIL'); manual line-by-line reading of every flagged file showed all 5 were parsing artifacts, not real defects -- true handshake integrity across all 41 manifest/verdict pairs is intact.
