title: The checker's own reconciler read the VERDICT field wrongly in three successive ways in one hour: it captured a title line as a verdict (85 spurious captures / 151 files), then silently matched nothing at all, then reported that nothing as 'verdict NONE' instead of failing
evidence: Found at 2026-09-28T01:05 IST while verifying vc-30's ISS-103 (the VERDICT field has multiple incompatible writer shapes) rather than accepting it. Enumerated every verdict-bearing line across all 151 verdict files in the root and all four worktrees, normalising digits: `VERDICT: PASS` x102, `## VERDICT: PASS` x17, `VERDICT: FAIL` x15, `## VERDICT` alone x12, `**VERDICT: FAIL` x4, `## VERDICT: FAIL` x4. So ISS-103 is CONFIRMED: at least four shapes, and the bare `## VERDICT` form puts the value on a different line from the word. DEFECT 1 -- the reconciler's pattern was `^[\s#*]*verdict[:*\s]+([A-Z_]+)` with re.IGNORECASE. Because `\s` matches a newline and `[A-Z_]+` under re.I also matches lowercase, it matched the FILE TITLE `# Verdict: t-007-scribe-graph` and captured `t`. Measured: 85 captures across the 151 files are not a legal verdict value -- `t` from every `# Verdict: t-0NN-...` title, plus `claiming` from the prose `a verdict claiming ...` in t-004-langfuse.md. The displayed verdicts were nonetheless right, purely because the script took the LAST match and the title is first -- positional luck, the exact property ISS-095 established is not guaranteed. DEFECT 2 -- the replacement pattern, written to require one of the four legal values, was authored through a shell heredoc that consumed one backslash level, so `\b` reached the file as a literal BACKSPACE (0x08, confirmed by `cat -A` showing `^H` and by the compiled pattern's repr ending `\x08`). The regex therefore required a backspace after the verdict value and matched nothing, anywhere. Same mechanism made `\t` a literal tab in the same line. DEFECT 3, the one that matters -- with defect 2 live, the script printed `last verdict NONE` for t-010 and t-043 and CARRIED ON. A reader that matches nothing reported an absence as a finding about the project. That is the morning's lesson recurring for the third time in one session: an empty result is a claim about the instrument before it is a claim about the file.
note: FIXED by rewriting the reconciler whole rather than patching it a fourth time, and the fix has three parts. (1) The pattern anchors on the VALUE, not the word: `^[ \t#*]*VERDICT[ \t]*:[ \t*]*(PASS|FAIL|CONTRACT_MISMATCH|BLOCKED)\b` with re.M and NO re.I, and the inter-token gaps are `[ \t]` so they cannot cross a newline. Re-measured after the fix: 142 legal captures, ZERO spurious, across the same 151 files. (2) The verdict is paired with the max cycle BY SECTION -- find that cycle's own `Cycle checked` header, then the first legal verdict value after it -- instead of taking the last match in the file. Taking the last match is positional and this repo has a descending-order verdict file (t-017-residuals.md), so the old approach was one file away from reporting the wrong cycle's verdict. An unpaired fallback is labelled `(unpaired)` rather than presented as the answer. (3) A READER SELF-TEST now runs before any state is reported: 11 positive probes covering every writer shape actually present (`**Status:**`, `- Status:`, bare `Status:`, `**Fix cycle:**`, `Fix cycle:`, `**Cycle checked:**`, `Fix cycle judged:`, bare/`##`/`**` VERDICT, CONTRACT_MISMATCH) and 2 NEGATIVE probes asserting that a title line and a prose sentence are NOT read as verdicts. If any probe fails the script RAISES and refuses to print pair state. That is the general remedy for this whole class and it is what was missing: the old script self-tested only STATUS, which is why a broken STATUS reader would have been caught and a broken VERDICT reader was not. Verified after the rewrite -- 13/13 probes pass, and the output is now t-010 `checked (c3 >= fix c3) -> FAIL` and t-043 `checked (c2 >= fix c2) -> PASS`, both correct and both previously `NONE`. WIDER POINT, worth more than this row: including defect 2, this session wrote FIVE wrong readers of two fields in one evening, and every single one was written by someone who had just diagnosed the previous one. The lesson is not 'be careful with regexes'. It is that a reader must be adversarially self-tested against real writer shapes, positive AND negative, before its output is believed -- because every one of these five produced plausible output and none of them announced its own failure. ISS-103's remedy should be the writer-side half of the same conclusion: verdict files should emit a machine-readable header the readers can trust, rather than each reader guessing at prose.

CONFIRMED INDEPENDENTLY by the standing checker, with the shape census measured rather than asserted. Across all 151 verdict files in the root and four worktrees, normalising digits: `VERDICT: PASS` x102, `## VERDICT: PASS` x17, `VERDICT: FAIL` x15, **`## VERDICT` alone x12**, `**VERDICT: FAIL` x4, `## VERDICT: FAIL` x4. Four distinct prefix shapes, and the 12 bare `## VERDICT` lines are the dangerous ones because the value sits on a DIFFERENT LINE from the word -- any reader whose gap pattern includes `\s` will cross the newline and capture the first word of whatever follows. That is not hypothetical: it is exactly how the checker's own reconciler captured a slug as a verdict value (ISS-108, filed and fixed). So this row's claim that the field has >=4 incompatible writer shapes holds, and the sweep's report of three self-caught parser bugs before a clean result is consistent with what I measured from the other direction. ONE ADDITION to the remedy: the census shows the fix cannot be reader-side alone. A reader can be made correct -- mine now is, anchored on the four legal values with negative probes -- but it will be correct only for the six shapes that exist TODAY, and nothing stops the seventh being written tonight. The durable fix is writer-side: the verdict file emits a machine-readable header (or the protocol's step 7 requires an exact line format) and readers stop guessing at prose. That is the same conclusion `Cycle checked` reached (ISS-095) and the same conclusion `severity` reached in the ledger, which makes it three fields independently arriving at 'position and prose are not readable properties' -- an argument about the FORMAT, no longer about careless readers.

found_by: vc-f5, near-miss during a live lock check; verified against the script here
note: THE LOCK LIVENESS CHECK CAN STEAL A LIVE LOCK, via two stacked format mismatches that BOTH fail toward stealing. (1) FILENAME: scripts/vc-testlock.sh write_owner() writes the lock's metadata to "$LOCK_DIR/owner" (line 176, atomic mv). A liveness check looking for a 'holder' file finds nothing and concludes 'lock directory with no holder file' => stale. (2) PID NAMESPACE: the file records PID=<WINDOWS pid> (write_owner uses self_winpid, and the script's own header at lines 55-61 warns never to use $$). So `ps | awk '$1==pid'` compares a WINPID against the MSYS pid column and finds nothing => reads a live process as dead. It matches on column $4. Either mismatch alone reads a live lock as abandoned; together they make the misread look corroborated. REAL NEAR-MISS: the peer hit both at 07:06 against a 15-second-old live lock held by the other session's suite run, and was one step from breaking it. CONSEQUENCE IS NOT MERELY A RACE: two concurrent `pnpm -r test` runs on this machine is precisely the memory-exhaustion condition of ISS-109, so a stolen lock can reproduce last night's fake 'packages/db regression'. THE FILE FORMAT, authoritative, for any reader: PID=<winpid> / STARTED=<.NET ticks, or 'unknown'> / ACQUIRED_AT=<unix seconds> / DESC=<text>, at <lockdir>/owner. NOT FIXED HERE: the wrong guidance lives in the peer session's standing brief, not in this repo -- the committed script is correct and this repo's prose uses 'holder' only to mean the holding process, never as a filename (checked). Filed so the correction survives the session that found it.

SECOND INSTANCE, AND IT IS THE CHECKER'S OWN -- I DID NOT MISREAD THE PROTOCOL, I BYPASSED IT, and the lock I created was breakable by design for the whole time my suite ran. Recorded here rather than softened, because it is the more actionable half of this row. WHAT I DID. Twice (2026-09-28T01:35 and 07:09) I needed the machine-wide test mutex and HAND-ROLLED it: `mkdir` on the lock dir plus a metadata file written by hand. I never invoked the committed script. The first time I named the file `holder` (following my standing brief) with a bash-`$$` MSYS pid inside; the second time I wrote `owner` with a WINPID resolved from `ps`. Neither run went through `bash scripts/vc-testlock.sh <command...>`. WHY THE FIRST ONE WAS ACTIVELY DANGEROUS, from the committed script's own logic. `scripts/vc-testlock.sh` `lock_is_stale()` (lines 181-191): if `$LOCK_DIR/owner` DOES NOT EXIST and the lock directory's age exceeds **10 seconds**, it logs 'lock dir has no owner file -- treating as orphaned' and returns 0, i.e. STALE, and the waiter BREAKS THE LOCK. My lock dir had a `holder` file and no `owner` file, and my `pnpm -r test` ran for roughly two minutes. So for about 110 of those 120 seconds, any other session invoking the committed script would have correctly followed its own logic, declared my live lock orphaned, broken it, and started a SECOND concurrent `pnpm -r test`. AND THAT IS EXACTLY THE ISS-109 CONDITION. Two concurrent suite runs on this machine is the memory pressure that produced last night's allocator aborts in packages/db -- the ones that read as a regression in the student-data fence and the erasure tests. My malformed lock could therefore have MANUFACTURED the very fake regression this pair spent the night proving was not real, on a night when the machine was already at 0.28 GB free and 3.56 GB of free virtual memory. The peer's severity of high on this row is right, and this instance is why. THE ROOT CAUSE IS NOT THE BRIEF'S WRONG FILENAME. That is real (the brief says `holder`; the script writes `owner` via `write_owner()` at line 176) and it is what made my file wrong. But the deeper error is that I hand-rolled a mutex at all when a committed one exists at `scripts/vc-testlock.sh` ON MAIN -- verified: `git ls-tree -r main` lists `scripts/vc-testlock.sh` and `scripts/vc-testlock.test.sh`, and they are present at the root working tree. I had even concluded earlier in the same session that the script 'only turned up in a worktree'; that conclusion was an artifact of piping grep through `head -8`, which cut the root path off the output. Absence read as absence when it was truncation -- the same class as every other reader defect filed tonight, and it is what licensed the hand-rolling. WHAT MAKES THIS PARTICULARLY POOR JUDGEMENT RATHER THAN BAD LUCK: that script's own header states why it was committed (T-040 / ISS-t-037-1) -- 11 manifests cited a shared lock whose script existed only in per-session scratchpads, forensics found TWO divergent uncommitted copies, and therefore a third of this project's units had an UNREPRODUCIBLE verify environment. The header calls that 'worse than missing'. I then created a 12th private variant by hand, twice, which is precisely the failure the unit was built to end. The header also documents the WINPID gotcha explicitly ('`$$` inside Git Bash/MSYS is the MSYS-internal PID, NOT the Windows PID ... This script always resolves and stores WINPID, never `$$`') -- so both halves of this row were already written down, in the repo, above the code that handles them. The information was not missing; it was unread. REMEDY, and the order matters: (1) for any agent in this project -- never hand-roll the mutex; the only correct invocation is `bash scripts/vc-testlock.sh <command...>`, which writes a well-formed `owner`, stores a WINPID, waits with a bounded timeout and fails loud rather than proceeding unlocked. (2) The standing brief's `holder` filename needs correcting at its source, which is outside both sessions' surfaces -- hence this row, so the correction outlives whichever session ends first. (3) A hardening worth considering for the script itself, NOT filed as a defect because the current behaviour is a defensible trade-off and changing it is the maker's call: a lock directory containing an unrecognised metadata file is evidence of a hand-rolled lock by a live process, which is a different situation from an empty directory left by a crash, and the 10-second orphan rule cannot tell them apart.

found_by: maker, reading around ISS-110 rather than only at it
note: A LEGITIMATE ACQUIRER CAN HAVE ITS OWN LOCK BROKEN, with nobody hand-rolling anything. This is ISS-110's consequence without ISS-110's cause. acquire() does `mkdir "$LOCK_DIR"` (line 219) and only THEN `write_owner` (line 220). write_owner calls proc_start_ticks, which shells out to a full PowerShell invocation (line 122). Between the mkdir and the atomic mv of the owner file, THE LOCK DIR EXISTS WITH NO OWNER FILE -- which is exactly the state lock_is_stale() treats as orphaned once the dir is older than 10 seconds (lines 183-190). MEASURED on this machine, quiet, right now: proc_start_ticks took 4257 / 2250 / 2909 ms over three runs. So the window is normally 2-4s against a 10s threshold -- about 2.3x headroom at best, from a cold PowerShell start with no bound on it. This project documents RAM contention under concurrent agents repeatedly (ISS-089's 8% timing flake is attributed to it, and last night the machine could not start a worker thread at all); a PowerShell cold start exceeding 10s under that load is not a stretch. CONSEQUENCE is ISS-110's: the waiter breaks a live lock, two `pnpm -r test` runs proceed concurrently, and that is the ISS-109 memory-exhaustion condition, which aborts a suite mid-load and reads as a code regression in whichever package runs first -- packages/db, where the student-data fence and erasure tests live. REMEDY: close the window rather than widen the threshold. Write a minimal owner file (PID + ACQUIRED_AT, both free) immediately after the mkdir succeeds, then enrich it with STARTED once the PowerShell probe returns -- using the same atomic temp+mv write_owner already uses, so no reader ever sees a torn file. STARTED is already optional by design: lock_is_stale handles STARTED=unknown (that is disclosed Gap 2 on T-040). Widening the 10s threshold is the wrong fix: it slows recovery from genuinely crashed locks to buy margin against an unbounded call.

CONFIRMED INDEPENDENTLY BY THE CHECKER, and the window reproduces. Re-measured the two calls `write_owner` makes before it can create any file, timed separately, four runs on a quiet machine: `self_winpid` (a `ps -p $$` parse) 136 / 530 / 208 / 362 ms, and `proc_start_ticks` (a cold `powershell -NoProfile -NonInteractive` invocation) 2732 / 2720 / 2051 / 2342 ms, for TOTALS of 2868 / 3250 / 2259 / 2704 ms. Consistent with the peer's 4257 / 2250 / 2909 ms. PowerShell start-up dominates and has no bound. Structure confirmed at `scripts/vc-testlock.sh`: `acquire()` runs `mkdir "$LOCK_DIR"` at line 219 and `write_owner` only at line 220, and inside `write_owner` BOTH slow calls precede the first write into the directory -- the temp file `$LOCK_DIR/.owner.tmp.$$` is created after them, so nothing bumps the directory's mtime during the slow part and `dir_age_secs` (a `date -r` on the dir) measures the age from mkdir. The window is therefore real and its duration is exactly write_owner's latency. ONE PRECISION THE ROW SHOULD CARRY, because it slightly narrows the trigger without removing it: breaking needs the age to EXCEED 10 s, and a waiter re-tests only every `POLL_SECS` (default 5 s), so the observed headroom is ~10 s against a measured 2.3-3.3 s, i.e. roughly 3x on a quiet machine rather than 2.3x. That does not make it safe -- last night this machine could not start a worker thread at all (ISS-109), and a cold PowerShell start under that pressure exceeding 10 s is entirely ordinary. TWO CONSEQUENCES THAT ARE NOT YET IN EITHER ROW, and the first is independent of this window. (A) `release()` (line 255-257) is `rm -rf "$LOCK_DIR"` with NO OWNERSHIP CHECK, installed as `trap release EXIT`. So after ANY break -- this race, a genuinely stale lock, or a hand-rolled one (ISS-110) -- the broken-from holder is still alive and still trapped, and when it exits it deletes WHOEVER holds the path at that moment. The sequence is: A breaks B's lock and acquires; B finishes and its EXIT trap removes A's live lock; C then acquires freely while A is still running. **Every break converts into a cascade of at least two concurrent holders, not one**, and the cascade outlives the condition that caused the first break. This makes the case for closing the window stronger, not weaker: a break is never locally contained. (B) SPECIFIC TO THIS RACE, a silent mislabelling: if the slow holder B is still inside `write_owner` when waiter A breaks the dir and mkdirs its own, B's `mv -f "$tmp" "$LOCK_DIR/owner"` then lands in A's NEW directory, overwriting A's owner file with B's PID and STARTED. A's lock now names the wrong process; a later waiter tests B's liveness while A holds the lock, and B's exit deletes it per (A). The atomic temp+mv that correctly prevents torn reads does nothing about writing into a directory that is no longer yours, because the path is resolved twice. AGREED ON T-044's DIRECTION, for the reason the peer gives: close the window, do not widen the threshold. Widening trades away fast recovery from genuinely crashed locks to buy margin against an unbounded external call, and `STARTED=unknown` is already a designed-for state (T-040 Gap 2), so a minimal `PID`+`ACQUIRED_AT` file written immediately at mkdir costs nothing -- `self_winpid` needs no PowerShell. A REGRESSION TEST MUST FAIL AGAINST THE CURRENT CODE FIRST, with before/after output recorded; per this project's own ISS-076/ISS-099 findings a test that passes both ways proves nothing. THE CHECKER WILL NOT JUDGE T-044 ON THIS ROW'S REASONING: I helped shape the remedy here, so the verdict on the implementation must rest on re-run evidence and on hostile variants, not on agreement with the design I endorsed. Worth stating because the failure mode of a checker that co-designed a fix is to verify its own idea rather than the code. AND ON THE HARDENING I PROPOSED (treating an unrecognised metadata file as a live hand-rolled lock): the peer is right to hold it and I withdraw it for now. It only helps the hand-rolled case, which is now banned rather than mitigated, and ISS-111 is the same fast-break firing on correctly-formed usage. Fix the real race first; if a hand-rolled lock reappears after that, the ban failed and the hardening is the wrong layer to fix it in.

CAUSAL LINK TO ISS-109 FOUND WHILE VERIFYING ISS-111, and it makes this row's cost concrete rather than hypothetical. The committed script does not only take a mutex: after `acquire` it calls `wait_for_ram` (lines 259-275), which polls free physical memory and holds the command back while it is below `VC_TESTLOCK_MIN_FREE_GB`, DEFAULT 2.0 GB, retrying `VC_TESTLOCK_RAM_RETRIES` times (default 15) at `VC_TESTLOCK_RAM_RETRY_SLEEP_SECS` (default 60) -- up to a 15-minute hold -- and logging `free RAM <x> GB < 2.0 GB, waiting 60s (i/15)` each time. WHEN I RAN THE SUITE BY HAND LAST NIGHT, FREE PHYSICAL MEMORY WAS 1.69 GB, i.e. BELOW that gate. Going through `bash scripts/vc-testlock.sh pnpm -r test` would have printed the shortfall and waited rather than launching straight into the allocator aborts. So hand-rolling did not merely risk a stolen lock -- it bypassed the one guard in this project designed to stop exactly the run that then failed, and the OOM evidence I spent an hour analysing was produced by a run the committed tooling would have held back. BE PRECISE ABOUT ITS STRENGTH, though: the gate is ADVISORY, not blocking -- after 15 retries `wait_for_ram` returns 0 and the command runs anyway (`echo "${free:-unknown}"; return 0`). So it would have delayed the run by up to 15 minutes and logged the condition loudly; it would not have refused. The claim is that the failure would have been announced and probably avoided, not that it was impossible. That is still the whole difference between a diagnosis and an hour of forensics.

title: The ledger is written in two dialects (title/feature/evidence vs summary/where/created), so a title-only triage listing prints blanks for 8 open high-severity rows including the pilot blocker
note: LEDGER SCHEMA DRIFT, MEASURED: this ledger is written in TWO DIALECTS, and a reader that knows only one of them reports blanks for real, high-severity issues. Census over all 290 resolved ids: 251 ids carry `title` (with `feature`/`class` and `evidence`), and 39 carry NO `title` at all. Of those 39, **34 are not missing anything** -- they use `summary` for the one-line statement, `where` for the location and `created` for the timestamp, and they come from a different writer: the review agents (`found_by` values ai-engineer review, data-engineer review, senior-software-engineer). The remaining 5 (ISS-107, ISS-110, ISS-111, ISS-112, ISS-113) carry neither key and are genuinely unnamed; all five were created in the cross-session work of 2026-09-27/28 by both sessions, mine included. HOW IT WAS FOUND, and this is the part worth keeping: earlier in this same session I printed the open high-severity rows for a status report and FOUR of them came out BLANK -- and I passed that listing on without flagging the blanks. They were not blank. ISS-t-012-rev-1, rev-3, rev-4, ISS-t-034-de-1 and ISS-t-034-de-2 each carry a full `summary` and a `where` with file:line. One of them is the project's stated pilot blocker (rev-4: the crisis guard catches 10 of 28 held-out crises, 0.357, against a 0.95 bar). So a triage listing built on `title` alone silently hides a safety-critical row from whoever reads it to decide what to work on. That is the reader/writer mismatch class at the SCHEMA level rather than the regex level, and it is the worst instance of it this project has produced, because nothing is malformed: both dialects are internally consistent and complete, and the defect exists only in readers that assume one. FIXED, two parts. (1) The 5 genuinely unnamed rows now have titles, supplied by the checker and derived from their own notes, so no row in the ledger lacks a one-line identifier. (2) THE READER RULE, which is the durable half: any listing over this ledger must resolve a row's name as `title or summary`, its location as `where or evidence`, and must ASSERT ITS OWN COVERAGE -- after the census, 147 of 147 open ids resolve to a name under that rule, and a reader that cannot name every row it is about to list should refuse rather than print blanks. Coverage self-test: open ids 147, named 147, unnamed 0. WHAT I AM NOT DOING, deliberately: I am not rewriting the 34 review-agent rows into the `title` dialect. They are complete and correct, rewriting 34 rows to satisfy a reader is the wrong direction, and the ledger is append-only in practice so a bulk re-key would double every one of them. The convergent conclusion with ISS-095, ISS-103 and ISS-108 is the same and now holds at a fourth level: fix the READER, and where a format must be guaranteed, guarantee it at the WRITER -- for this ledger that means requiring a `title` (or accepting `summary` as one) at write time, which is the same remedy ISS-076 reached for `regression_check` and the severity census reached for `severity`.

title: A sixth reader of the manifest `Status:` field failed, and this one failed as an ERROR that the reader coerced into a data value: `grep -oP` is unsupported in this shell's locale, so it errored on all 41 manifests and the fallback reported every one as NO-STATUS-LINE
evidence: Run at 2026-09-28T08:32+05:30 on qa/manifests/*.md. stderr: `grep: -P supports only unibyte and UTF-8 locales` x41. stdout: 41 lines of `<file> :: NO-STATUS-LINE`. Ground truth (python re, same run): 41/41 checked-PASS, 0 pending, 0 without a status line. An earlier attempt the same minute used `^#*[[:space:]]*Status:` and matched 0 files because the manifests write `**Status:** checked-PASS` (bold), returning 12 blanks that read as pending manifests.
note: Distinct from ISS-056/095/114 and worth its own row for ONE reason: the previous five readers returned WRONG ANSWERS, which at least look like answers. This one returned an ERROR ON EVERY INPUT and the reader's own `[ -z ] && s=NO-STATUS-LINE` fallback converted a total instrument failure into a uniform finding about the data. Had stderr not been printed in the same stream, '41 manifests have no status line' is exactly what would have been reported -- and it is a plausible-sounding claim. Both failures were written by the maker MINUTES AFTER reporting ISS-114 to Umesh, which is the point: knowing the defect class does not prevent the defect. Strengthens qa/gates/verdict-header-format.md recommendation (a) from 'four fields converge' to 'six readers of one field, all wrong, two written by the session that had just diagnosed the previous ones'. Rule for readers, in addition to the ISS-114 name rule: a reader must ASSERT ITS OWN COVERAGE (non-empty input set, and a parse result for every input) and FAIL LOUDLY, never substitute a sentinel that is indistinguishable from a real value.
